A2.text:
Leyla is sixteen. She writes for her school newspaper in Sheki. She wants to be a journalist.

One Monday, there was a rumour in her street. “Uncle Rauf's bakery is closing!” people said. The gossip spread very fast on WhatsApp. Soon, it was the talk of the town. Everybody loves Uncle Rauf's bread, and people were very sad.

Leyla wanted the truth. Her teacher always said, “Take it with a pinch of salt. Check your source.”

First, Leyla asked who started the rumour. It was Mrs Zohra. But Mrs Zohra has a bakery too! Her story was biased.

Then Leyla found an eyewitness. Old Mr Javid lives next to the bakery. “I saw builders there yesterday,” he said. “They were not closing the shop. They were making it bigger!”

Finally, Leyla talked to Uncle Rauf. He laughed. “Closing? No! I am opening a café inside the bakery. People can drink tea with fresh bread.”

Leyla wrote an article. Her headline was: “Uncle Rauf's bakery is not closing — it's growing!” Her teacher did not censor anything.

Leyla was happy to break the news. The next morning, there was a long queue at the bakery. Uncle Rauf gave Leyla a free loaf of bread.

“Thank you,” he said. “Good journalists are better than gossip.”

questions.why: Leyla checks her sources and finds the bakery is growing.

options: Don't believe everything you hear immediately

questions.why: “Mrs Zohra has a bakery too! Her story was biased.”

B1.text:
Leyla, sixteen, was the youngest writer on her school newspaper in Sheki, and she took the job seriously. So when a rumour exploded on the neighbourhood WhatsApp group one Monday morning, she was more curious than worried.

“Rauf's bakery is closing at the end of the month!” the message said. By lunchtime, the gossip had spread to every family on the street. By the evening, it was the talk of the town. People who had bought Uncle Rauf's bread for thirty years were posting sad photos of his famous round loaves.

Leyla remembered her teacher's favourite advice: “Take everything with a pinch of salt until you've checked the source.”

So she started with the source. After three phone calls, she traced the first message to Mrs Zohra, who — interestingly — had opened a rival bakery two streets away last spring. Not exactly an unbiased witness.

Next, she looked for an eyewitness. Mr Javid, who had lived next to the bakery for forty years and noticed everything, was happy to help. “Closing? Nonsense. I saw builders going in yesterday with bags of cement and a new window.”

Finally, she went straight to Uncle Rauf himself. He was so surprised he dropped a tray of bread. “Closing? I'm expanding! I'm turning the back room into a tea house, so people can eat my bread while it's still warm.”

That night Leyla wrote her article. The headline read: “Sheki's favourite bakery isn't closing — it's growing.” She was worried the school director might censor the part about Mrs Zohra, but he didn't change a single word.

The next morning, she was proud to break the news to the whole street. By eight o'clock, the queue outside Uncle Rauf's bakery went round the corner.

When Leyla arrived, Uncle Rauf handed her a warm loaf wrapped in paper. “On the house,” he said. “For the girl who killed a rumour.”

B2.text:
At sixteen, Leyla was the youngest contributor to her school newspaper in Sheki, and she treated the position with the gravity of a foreign correspondent. So when a rumour detonated on the neighbourhood WhatsApp group one Monday morning, her reaction was less alarm than professional interest.

“Rauf's bakery is shutting down at the end of the month!” the message announced. By lunchtime, the gossip had spread to every household on the street; by evening, it was the talk of the town. Customers who had bought Uncle Rauf's bread for three decades were posting mournful photographs of his famous round loaves, as if composing an obituary.

Leyla recalled her teacher's favourite maxim: “Take everything with a pinch of salt until you know the source.”

So she began with the source. Three phone calls later, she had traced the original message to Mrs Zohra — who, as it happened, had opened a rival bakery two streets away the previous spring. Hardly the most impartial of witnesses; if anything, her account was spectacularly biased.

Next, Leyla sought an eyewitness. Mr Javid, who had lived beside the bakery for forty years and missed nothing, was delighted to be consulted. “Closing? Rubbish. Yesterday I watched builders carry in sacks of cement and an enormous new window frame.”

Finally, she went straight to Uncle Rauf. The question startled him so badly that he nearly dropped a tray of loaves. “Closing? I'm expanding! I'm converting the back room into a tea house, so people can eat my bread while it's still warm.”

That night Leyla wrote her article under the headline “Sheki's favourite bakery isn't closing — it's growing.” She half expected the school director to censor the paragraph naming the origin of the rumour, but he approved it without altering a word.

The next morning, she had the considerable satisfaction of being the one to break the news to the whole street. By eight o'clock, the queue outside the bakery stretched round the corner.

When Leyla arrived, Uncle Rauf pressed a warm loaf, wrapped in paper, into her hands. “On the house,” he said. “For the young lady who killed a rumour with three phone calls and a question.”
